question: Which test is most commonly used to determine whether an item has become a fixture and thus real property?
choice_a: The method of attachment, adaptability to the property's use, and the intent of the party who installed it
choice_b: The original purchase price of the item
choice_c: Whether the item can be lifted by one person
choice_d: The color and style of the item compared to the rest of the room
explanation: Courts weigh the method and permanence of attachment, adaptation of the item to the real property's use, and the intent of the annexor when determining whether personal property has become a fixture.

question: A tenant installs custom shelving in a rented retail space solely to display merchandise for their business. How is this item classified?
choice_a: A real property fixture that automatically transfers to the landlord
choice_b: A trade fixture, which remains the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease ends
choice_c: An encumbrance on the landlord's title
choice_d: A riparian right
explanation: Trade fixtures installed by a tenant for conducting business are treated as personal property and generally may be removed by the tenant before the lease expires, provided the tenant repairs any resulting damage.

question: What is the key legal difference between real property and personal property when transferring ownership?
choice_a: Personal property must always be conveyed by deed
choice_b: Real property can only be transferred through a will
choice_c: Real property is conveyed by deed, while personal property is conveyed by bill of sale
choice_d: There is no legal difference; both use identical transfer documents
explanation: Real property (land and things permanently attached to it) is conveyed using a deed, while personal property (movable items, or chattels) is conveyed using a bill of sale.

question: A legal description of land using metes and bounds begins at a fixed reference point. What is this starting point called?
choice_a: The benchmark
choice_b: The principal meridian
choice_c: The point of curvature
choice_d: The point of beginning
explanation: A metes and bounds description starts at the point of beginning (POB), then traces the property's boundary lines by direction (bearing) and distance until returning to the POB.

question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, what is the size of one standard section of land?
choice_a: 640 acres, or one square mile
choice_b: 160 acres
choice_c: 36 square miles
choice_d: 43,560 square feet
explanation: A township is divided into 36 sections, each one square mile and containing 640 acres. A quarter section would contain 160 acres.

question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, how many sections make up a standard township?
choice_a: 24 sections
choice_b: 36 sections arranged in a 6-by-6 grid
choice_c: 4 sections
choice_d: 100 sections
explanation: A township is a square parcel measuring six miles on each side, divided into 36 numbered sections of one square mile each.

question: How many square feet are in one acre of land?
choice_a: 5,280 square feet
choice_b: 10,000 square feet
choice_c: 43,560 square feet
choice_d: 36,000 square feet
explanation: One acre equals 43,560 square feet, a standard conversion used throughout real estate math and land measurement.

question: Which legal description method identifies a parcel by referencing a numbered lot within a subdivision map filed with the county?
choice_a: Metes and bounds
choice_b: Government rectangular survey
choice_c: Datum reference system
choice_d: Lot and block (recorded plat) system
explanation: The lot and block system references a specific lot number and block number shown on a recorded subdivision plat map on file with the county recorder, commonly used for platted residential subdivisions.

question: When appraisers or agents measure a home's gross living area (GLA), what space is typically included?
choice_a: Finished, heated living space above grade, measured from exterior wall surfaces
choice_b: Unfinished basement space only
choice_c: The total lot size including the yard
choice_d: Garage and unheated attic space
explanation: Gross living area generally refers to finished, habitable above-grade space measured from the exterior walls; unfinished basements, garages, and unheated areas are typically excluded or reported separately.

question: A permanent reference marker of known location and elevation, used by surveyors to establish other measurements, is called a:
choice_a: Monument
choice_b: Benchmark
choice_c: Datum
choice_d: Meridian
explanation: A benchmark is a permanent marker of known position and elevation used as a reference point by surveyors; a monument is a fixed natural or artificial object marking a boundary corner.

question: What is a lien?
choice_a: A written promise to sell property at a future date
choice_b: A form of joint ownership between two or more parties
choice_c: A financial claim or charge against a property that secures the payment of a debt or obligation
choice_d: A physical intrusion of a structure onto a neighboring lot
explanation: A lien is an encumbrance that gives a creditor a legal claim against property as security for a debt, such as a mortgage lien, tax lien, or mechanic's lien.

question: Which type of lien attaches to all real and personal property owned by a debtor, rather than to one specific property?
choice_a: A specific lien
choice_b: A mechanic's lien
choice_c: A mortgage lien
choice_d: A general lien
explanation: A general lien, such as a judgment lien or estate tax lien, attaches to all property a debtor owns. A specific lien, like a mortgage or mechanic's lien, attaches only to a particular property.

question: A contractor who has not been paid for work performed on a property may file which type of lien to secure payment?
choice_a: A mechanic's lien
choice_b: A judgment lien
choice_c: An estate tax lien
choice_d: An easement
explanation: A mechanic's lien is a specific, involuntary lien filed by contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers who have not been paid for labor or materials furnished to improve a property.

question: Which of the following best describes a voluntary lien?
choice_a: A lien imposed by a court after a lawsuit judgment
choice_b: A lien a property owner agrees to, such as a mortgage taken to purchase or refinance a home
choice_c: A lien placed by a government for unpaid property taxes
choice_d: A lien filed by an unpaid contractor
explanation: A voluntary lien is one the owner willingly enters into, most commonly a mortgage; involuntary liens (tax liens, judgment liens, mechanic's liens) are imposed without the owner's consent.

question: Generally, how is priority among multiple liens on the same property determined?
choice_a: By the dollar amount of the lien, with the largest lien always paid first
choice_b: By the type of lienholder's profession
choice_c: By the order in which the liens were recorded, with earlier-recorded liens typically taking priority
choice_d: Priority is always decided by a jury trial
explanation: Lien priority is generally established by recording date, on a first-recorded, first-paid basis, though property tax liens typically take superior priority regardless of recording date.

question: What is an easement?
choice_a: A form of concurrent ownership between spouses
choice_b: A temporary permission to be on land that can be revoked at any time
choice_c: A structure that physically intrudes onto a neighbor's property
choice_d: A nonpossessory right to use another person's land for a specific purpose
explanation: An easement is a nonpossessory interest giving someone the right to use another's land for a defined purpose, such as access or utility lines, without granting ownership.

question: An easement appurtenant benefits one parcel of land (the dominant estate) and burdens another (the servient estate). What happens to this easement when the dominant estate is sold?
choice_a: It automatically transfers with the dominant estate to the new owner
choice_b: It terminates immediately upon sale
choice_c: It must be renegotiated with the servient estate owner
choice_d: It converts into an easement in gross
explanation: An easement appurtenant runs with the land, meaning it automatically transfers to successive owners of the dominant estate and continues to burden the servient estate.

question: A utility company holds the right to run power lines across a private parcel, a right that benefits the utility company rather than any adjoining land. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement appurtenant
choice_b: An easement in gross
choice_c: An easement by necessity
choice_d: A license
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a person or entity (such as a utility company) rather than a neighboring parcel of land, and there is no dominant estate.

question: What distinguishes a license from an easement in real property law?
choice_a: A license lasts forever, while an easement expires after one year
choice_b: A license must be recorded, while an easement never needs to be recorded
choice_c: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use land, while an easement is a legal interest that generally runs with the land
choice_d: There is no meaningful difference between the two
explanation: A license is merely permission to use land that can be revoked at the will of the owner and does not run with the land, unlike an easement, which is a durable property interest.

question: A landowner whose parcel has no access to a public road except by crossing a neighbor's land may be entitled to which type of easement?
choice_a: An easement in gross
choice_b: A license
choice_c: An encroachment
choice_d: An easement by necessity
explanation: An easement by necessity is created by courts to provide legal access to a landlocked parcel, typically arising when a larger tract is subdivided and one resulting lot has no road frontage.

question: What is an encroachment?
choice_a: A physical structure or improvement, such as a fence or roof overhang, that unlawfully extends onto a neighboring property
choice_b: A right to use another's land for access
choice_c: A written agreement transferring mineral rights
choice_d: A type of concurrent ownership
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a physical improvement, such as a fence, driveway, or building, extends across a boundary line onto an adjoining owner's property without permission.

question: A survey is often ordered before closing primarily to detect which type of issue?
choice_a: The buyer's creditworthiness
choice_b: Encroachments and boundary line discrepancies
choice_c: The seller's marital status
choice_d: The property's fair market rental value
explanation: A boundary survey identifies the precise location of property lines and can reveal encroachments, such as a neighbor's fence or structure crossing onto the subject property.

question: How can adverse possession potentially result in a person acquiring legal title to land they do not own?
choice_a: By simply paying the property taxes for one year
choice_b: By recording a deed prepared by the possessor
choice_c: By openly, notoriously, continuously, and exclusively occupying the land without the true owner's permission for a statutory period
choice_d: By obtaining a license from the owner
explanation: Adverse possession allows a possessor who occupies land openly, notoriously, continuously, exclusively, and often hostilely (without the owner's permission) for a period set by state law to potentially gain legal title.

question: A property that is subject to an ongoing probate proceeding after the owner's death is an example of a potential encumbrance because:
choice_a: Probate automatically extinguishes all existing liens on the property
choice_b: Probate converts the property into personal property
choice_c: Probate proceedings have no effect on real property title
choice_d: Clear title cannot typically be conveyed until the estate is administered and the court authorizes transfer
explanation: When an owner dies, the property may need to pass through probate, and marketable title generally cannot be conveyed until the estate is settled or the court approves the transfer.

question: How does an existing lease affect a buyer purchasing rental property?
choice_a: The buyer generally takes title subject to the existing lease, and the tenant's rights continue under the new owner
choice_b: All leases automatically terminate the moment title transfers
choice_c: The tenant must immediately vacate upon sale
choice_d: The lease becomes void and must be entirely renegotiated
explanation: An existing lease is a potential encumbrance because the new owner typically takes the property subject to the tenant's leasehold rights, honoring the lease terms until it expires.

question: What are mineral rights?
choice_a: The right to build structures above a certain height
choice_b: The right to extract subsurface resources such as oil, gas, coal, or other minerals, which can be sold or leased separately from the surface estate
choice_c: The right to use water flowing across adjoining land
choice_d: A form of leasehold estate
explanation: Mineral rights allow the holder to extract subsurface resources and can be severed from surface rights, meaning one party may own the surface while another owns the minerals beneath it.

question: What are air rights?
choice_a: The right to draw water from a stream bordering the property
choice_b: The right to mine subsurface minerals
choice_c: The right to use, develop, or control the open space above a parcel of land, which can be sold or transferred independently
choice_d: A type of easement in gross
explanation: Air rights refer to the space above a property and can be sold, leased, or transferred separately from surface and subsurface rights, commonly used in dense urban development.

question: Under the riparian rights doctrine, landowners whose property borders a flowing waterway, such as a river or stream, generally have:
choice_a: Exclusive ownership of the entire waterway regardless of other landowners
choice_b: No rights to the water whatsoever
choice_c: Rights determined solely by whichever owner arrived first, regardless of location
choice_d: Reasonable use of the adjacent water, shared with other riparian owners along the same waterway
explanation: Riparian rights give owners of land bordering a flowing waterway reasonable use of the water shared among all riparian landowners along that watercourse, distinct from prior appropriation systems used in some Western states.

question: Littoral rights apply to landowners whose property borders which type of body of water?
choice_a: Large, non-flowing bodies of water such as oceans, seas, and lakes
choice_b: Underground aquifers only
choice_c: Man-made irrigation canals exclusively
choice_d: Seasonal drainage ditches
explanation: Littoral rights belong to owners of land bordering large, generally non-flowing bodies of water such as oceans, seas, and lakes, and typically extend ownership to the high-water mark.

question: What is ownership in severalty?
choice_a: Ownership shared equally by exactly two people
choice_b: Ownership of property by one individual or single legal entity
choice_c: Ownership that automatically includes a right of survivorship
choice_d: Ownership held by a married couple only
explanation: Severalty ownership means the property is owned by one person or a single legal entity (such as a corporation), separate and severed from ownership by others.

question: In a tenancy in common, what happens to a co-owner's interest in the property when that co-owner dies?
choice_a: It automatically transfers to the surviving co-owners by right of survivorship
choice_b: The entire property must be sold immediately upon any co-owner's death
choice_c: It passes to the deceased owner's heirs or according to their will, not automatically to the surviving co-owners
choice_d: It reverts to the original grantor
explanation: Tenants in common do not have a right of survivorship; each owner's interest passes to their heirs or as directed by their will, and co-owners may hold unequal shares.

question: Joint tenancy with right of survivorship is distinguished from tenancy in common primarily by which feature?
choice_a: Joint tenants may own unequal percentage shares
choice_b: Joint tenancy can only be created between family members
choice_c: Joint tenancy requires a written lease agreement
choice_d: Upon a joint tenant's death, their interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s) rather than to heirs
explanation: The defining feature of joint tenancy is the right of survivorship, meaning a deceased joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s), bypassing probate and the deceased's will.

question: Traditionally, creating a valid joint tenancy requires the presence of the four unities. Which of the following correctly names these unities?
choice_a: Time, title, interest, and possession
choice_b: Price, location, size, and zoning
choice_c: Marriage, age, residency, and citizenship
choice_d: Recording, notarization, witnessing, and delivery
explanation: The four unities required to create a joint tenancy at common law are unity of time (interests acquired at the same time), title (same deed or document), interest (equal shares), and possession (equal right to use the whole property).

question: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of concurrent ownership available specifically to:
choice_a: Any group of three or more unrelated investors
choice_b: Married couples, and includes a right of survivorship in most jurisdictions that recognize it
choice_c: Corporations only
choice_d: Tenants renting under a month-to-month lease
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a special form of joint ownership reserved for married couples in states that recognize it, providing a right of survivorship and, in many states, added protection from creditors of only one spouse.

question: What is a condominium form of ownership?
choice_a: A corporation owns the entire building, and residents own shares of stock plus a proprietary lease
choice_b: A single owner leases individual units to multiple tenants
choice_c: Individual ownership of a unit combined with an undivided share of ownership in the common areas of the property
choice_d: Ownership limited strictly to one week's use of a property per year
explanation: In a condominium, each owner holds fee simple title to their individual unit and, together with other unit owners, an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the building's common areas and land.

question: In a cooperative (co-op) form of ownership, what does a resident actually own?
choice_a: Fee simple title to their individual unit
choice_b: An undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the land only
choice_c: A recorded easement over the building
choice_d: Shares of stock in the corporation that owns the building, along with a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit
explanation: Cooperative ownership involves a corporation holding title to the entire building; residents purchase shares of stock in that corporation and receive a proprietary lease giving them the right to occupy a specific unit.

question: A timeshare arrangement typically grants an owner which type of interest in a property?
choice_a: The right to use or occupy the property for a specific, recurring period of time each year
choice_b: Full-time, exclusive fee simple ownership of the entire property
choice_c: A general lien against the property
choice_d: An easement in gross benefiting a neighboring parcel
explanation: A timeshare divides ownership or use rights among multiple parties, each entitled to occupy the property during a designated recurring interval, and may be structured as either fee ownership or a right-to-use arrangement.

question: When real property is held in trust, who holds legal title to the property on behalf of the beneficiary?
choice_a: The trustor's attorney
choice_b: The trustee
choice_c: The beneficiary directly
choice_d: The county recorder
explanation: In a trust arrangement, the trustee holds legal title to the property and manages it according to the trust's terms for the benefit of the beneficiary, who holds equitable title.

question: When a property owner dies without a will (intestate), how is real property in their estate typically transferred?
choice_a: It automatically becomes government property
choice_b: It is transferred by the nearest neighbor's claim
choice_c: According to the state's intestate succession laws, often through a probate court proceeding
choice_d: Ownership immediately vests in the deceased's real estate agent
explanation: When someone dies intestate (without a valid will), state intestate succession laws determine how the estate's real property passes to heirs, typically through probate administration.

question: Which business entity structure generally provides its owners (shareholders) with limited personal liability for the entity's real estate obligations?
choice_a: A general partnership
choice_b: Sole proprietorship
choice_c: Joint tenancy
choice_d: A corporation
explanation: A corporation is a separate legal entity that can hold title to real property, and shareholders generally enjoy limited liability, meaning their personal assets are shielded from the corporation's debts and obligations.

question: In a general partnership that owns real property, how is liability typically shared among the partners?
choice_a: Each general partner shares unlimited personal liability for the partnership's debts and obligations
choice_b: No partner bears any personal liability under any circumstances
choice_c: Liability is automatically capped at each partner's original investment
choice_d: Only the partnership entity itself, and never any partner, can be held liable
explanation: In a general partnership, all general partners share unlimited personal liability for partnership debts and obligations, unlike limited partners in a limited partnership or shareholders in a corporation.

question: A limited liability company (LLC) holding title to real estate combines which two features that make it attractive to real estate investors?
choice_a: Unlimited personal liability with corporate double taxation
choice_b: The limited liability protection similar to a corporation with the pass-through taxation typical of a partnership
choice_c: Mandatory public stock trading with no liability protection
choice_d: Government ownership with private management
explanation: An LLC is popular for holding real estate because it offers members limited liability protection while generally allowing pass-through taxation, avoiding the double taxation associated with standard corporations.

question: A conventional life estate grants an individual (the life tenant) the right to possess and use property for:
choice_a: A fixed term of 99 years regardless of life span
choice_b: As long as the life tenant continues to pay rent to a landlord
choice_c: The duration of their own life, after which the property passes to a remainderman or reverts to the original grantor
choice_d: Perpetuity, passing to the life tenant's heirs upon death
explanation: A life estate lasts for the duration of a measuring life (usually the life tenant's own life), after which title automatically passes to a named remainderman or reverts to the original grantor or their heirs.

question: A life estate measured by the lifetime of someone other than the life tenant is known as a life estate:
choice_a: In severalty
choice_b: In gross
choice_c: By the entirety
choice_d: Pur autre vie
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie ("for the life of another") is measured by the life of a person other than the life tenant, and it ends when that other named person dies.

question: When a life estate ends and full ownership automatically passes back to the original grantor (or the grantor's heirs) rather than to a third party, this future interest is called a:
choice_a: Reversion
choice_b: Remainder
choice_c: Encroachment
choice_d: License
explanation: A reversion is the future interest retained by the original grantor when property returns to them (or their estate) after a life estate ends; when it instead passes to a named third party, that interest is called a remainder.

question: What obligation does a life tenant generally have regarding the property during the life estate?
choice_a: No obligations whatsoever, since the life tenant owns the property outright
choice_b: The duty to maintain the property and avoid committing waste that would damage the interests of the remainderman or reversioner
choice_c: The obligation to sell the property within five years
choice_d: The duty to transfer full fee simple title to a lender
explanation: A life tenant must avoid committing waste, meaning they cannot allow the property to fall into disrepair or take actions that permanently diminish its value, protecting the interests of the remainderman or reversioner.

question: Community property is a form of marital property ownership recognized in certain states. Under a typical community property system, property acquired during the marriage is generally:
choice_a: Owned entirely by whichever spouse's name appears on the deed
choice_b: Automatically split 70/30 in favor of the higher-earning spouse
choice_c: Owned equally by both spouses, regardless of which spouse's income purchased it
choice_d: Excluded from any ownership claim by either spouse
explanation: In community property states, most property acquired by either spouse during the marriage is generally considered owned equally by both spouses, distinct from separate property owned before the marriage or received by gift or inheritance.

question: A planned unit development (PUD) typically combines individual fee simple ownership of a home and lot with what additional feature?
choice_a: Corporate stock ownership in place of a deed
choice_b: A revocable license to occupy the home
choice_c: Mandatory conversion to cooperative ownership after ten years
choice_d: Shared ownership responsibility, often through a homeowners association, for common amenities such as parks or recreational facilities
explanation: In a PUD, owners hold fee simple title to their individual lot and dwelling while also belonging to a homeowners association that owns and maintains shared common areas and amenities.

question: What is the primary practical difference between real property and personal property in terms of how each is affected by a sale of the land?
choice_a: Real property automatically transfers with the land unless excluded, while personal property does not transfer unless specifically included in the sale
choice_b: Personal property always transfers with the land automatically
choice_c: Neither real nor personal property ever transfers without a separate bill of sale
choice_d: Real property must be itemized separately in every contract, while personal property never needs to be
explanation: Because fixtures and other real property are legally part of the land, they convey automatically with a sale unless the contract specifically excludes them, whereas personal property (chattel) does not transfer unless expressly included.
